desc:
A single worker has to process jobs, where jobs[i] = [release, duration]. Job i becomes available at time release and cannot start earlier. The worker handles one job at a time, never interrupts a job, and may choose the order. The worker is allowed to wait idle when nothing is available yet.

Return the earliest possible time at which all jobs are done (0 if there are no jobs).

jobs = [[0, 3], [10, 2], [4, 1]]  ->  12
jobs = [[5, 2], [5, 3]]           ->  10

In the first example the worker does the jobs in release order: [0,3], then [4,5], then [10,12].
hints: Whatever order you choose, the worker can never finish before the latest release time plus the duration of that job.
Starting a job as soon as possible is always right, so the order is the only decision. What is the natural order if jobs only get unlocked over time?
Sort by release time and simulate: t = max(t, release) + duration for every job.
editorial: Process the jobs in order of release time. Keep the current time t; for each job the worker starts at max(t, release) (waiting if the job is not there yet) and finishes duration later.

Why it is optimal: the finish time of any schedule is at least release_j + (sum of durations of all jobs released at or after release_j) for every j, because all those jobs can only start once release_j has passed. Release order achieves the maximum of these bounds exactly, so no other order can beat it. Cost is O(n log n) for the sort.
